sources.citation: Man, Edward Horace. 1889. A Dictionary of the Central Nicobarese Language (English-Nicobarese and Nicobarese-English), with appendices containing a comparison of synonymous words in the remaining Nicobarese forms.. London: W.H. Allen.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Introduction: 'no instance has been discovered in any of the dialects in which the meaning of words depends on tone, accent, or emphasis'. The orthography key gives a stress rule ('In disyllabic words stress occurs on the second syllable unless there is a long vowel in the first syllable. In trisyllabic and polysyllabic words stress usually occurs on the penultimate syllable whenever neither or none of the other syllables have accented vowels') but this describes CENTRAL Nicobarese (Nancowry), the dictionary language; Chowra figures only in the comparative word appendix.

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul. 2022. A classification of the Nicobarese languages. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 15.1: 1-16.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Lexicostatistical/sound-correspondence classification; Chowra/Sanenyo data drawn from Man 1889, Rajasingh 2019 and Abbi & Pachori. No mention of stress, accent or prosody for any lect.

sources.citation: Abbi, Anvita & Rahul Pachori. 2020 [print ed. listed by SPPEL as 2023]. A Grammatical Sketch of Sanenyo spoken in Chowra, The Nicobar Islands, India. Mysuru: Scheme for Protection and Preservation of Endangered Languages, Central Institute of Indian Languages. 215 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Chapter 3 'The sound system of Sanenyo' (pp.29-46) read in full: vowels (7 oral + 6 nasal), length not phonemic, diphthongs, consonants, unreleased finals, syllable CV(C), clusters/gemination. There is NO section and no statement on word-stress/accent placement. Only a passing remark p.32 (sec. 3.4.3) that free variation is 'not due to the presence and absence of stressed syllables', and p.121 that yes/no questions carry 'high intonation'. No IPA stress marks anywhere in the transcriptions.

sources.citation: Abbi, Anvita & Rahul Pachori. 2020. Sanenyo Dictionary (Sanenyo-English-Hindi). Mysuru: SPPEL, CIIL. 542 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Preface pp.i-xiv (text layer font-garbled; scanned at 200 dpi ->). Phonology summary pp.vi-vii repeats the grammar's inventory (13 vowels, 16 consonants, unreleased final stops, no voiced stops, 'speakers speak amazingly fast'); nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul. 2018. Proto-Nicobarese phonology. In Hiram Ring & Felix Rau (eds), Papers from the Seventh International Conference on Austroasiatic Linguistics (JSEALS Special Publication 3), 101 ff. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: States iambic stress ('the rightmost syllable of lexical roots bears the primary word stress') explicitly for CAR Nicobarese (sec. 2.1.1) and discusses Nancowry; Chowra is known to him only from Man 1889's ~380-word appendix and 'the analyses and reconstruction.. are based primarily on just those two languages [Car, Nancowry]'. Nothing on Chowra prosody.
